newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Nestle's sees coffee price hikes eroding demand.
newsitem.headline: Nestle's sees coffee price hikes eroding demand.

text.p: The worldwide director of Nestle AG said he sees volatility in world coffee markets continuing for the foreseeble future and cautioned that price hikes are hurting consumption.

"Significant price volatility in the next few years is likely to be the rule rather than the exception," Mario Conti, director general of Nestle, told a meeting in this northwest industrial center marking the 70th anniversary of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation.

The reasons behind the expected volatility are various, Corti said, but he stressed the growing presence of "speculative funds" in the commodities market and "the fact that the safety net of quality stocks in consuming and producing countries no longer exists for all practical purposes."
Both of these factors contributed to the sharp runup in coffee prices earlier this year, he said, adding they were sure to hurt consumption -- especially in the United States and central Europe.

"Some sources presently estimate that North American consumption volume might drop by as much as 10 percent in 1997 compared to 1996," Corti said, insisting that there was a direct correlation between the price roasters have to pay for their raw material and consumption trends.

In Europe, he said this year's expected decline in consumption would probably be much less than in the United States. But he noted that the strengthening of the dollar against most European currencies "has aggravated the effect of higher green coffee prices when converting to selling prices in national currencies."

To underscore the link between prices and consumption, Corti said 1996 world coffee consumption -- including the 3,300 cups of Nestle coffee he said were being consumed every second around the globe -- was just 1.5 percent higher than in 1993.

"We should have expected -- under a stable price environment, and I emphasize stable not low -- a 3.0 percent increase," he said, citing a "price explosion" in mid-1994 as the main reason for lower-than-expected growth.

As for ways of creating a more stable environment, Corti said roasters and producers alike faced an "enormous challenge." But he appeared to put the onus on the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) in particular, urging it to show greater flexibility "in adpating their strategy to rectify short-term market disturbances."

"If a more constructive plan of action had been adopted in the last six months by the immediate release of stocks, much of the subsequent damage could have been avoided, and the ACPC cause would have gained in stature and credibility," Corti said.
Finally, he said Nestle believed robusta availability should be sufficient to satisfy the current 1.0 percent increase in world consumption annually.

He stressed, however, that "the forward availability of unwashed arabica coffees poses the greatest threat to the industry's ability to satisfy the consumer's desire for coffee variety instead of just one standard beverage."
